title: Automatic capture of contacts, meetings and emails into the firm's CRM
problem: Relationship data sits in individual inboxes and calendars because fee-earners rarely log contacts by hand, so the client relationship system is incomplete.
approach: Software reads email and calendars and updates CRM records automatically. Named: Schneider Downs, LBMC, KSM, Grassi, Thomson Snell & Passmore.
Introhive's case study says Schneider Downs ingested 3,120,627 meetings and emails and found 71,948 new contacts (vendor-published).
Professionals review newly found contacts before they enter the CRM; users set deny lists and keywords that block processing.
who: Schneider Downs, LBMC, KSM, Grassi, Introhive

title: Relationship maps and strength scores for warm paths and partner succession
problem: Firms cannot see who knows whom across practices, so cross-sell is missed, outreach is duplicated, and relationships can leave with departing partners.
approach: Captured data becomes relationship maps and strength scores for warm introductions and succession planning. Named: Thomson Snell & Passmore, Grassi, Howes Percival.
Introhive says Thomson Snell & Passmore's employees connected to top accounts rose from 47 to 97 (vendor-published).
Partners and business development staff decide whom to contact and what to say.
who: Thomson Snell & Passmore, Grassi, Howes Percival

title: Client-health scores and alerts when a relationship cools
problem: Relationship owners lose touch, miss job changes and news, and notice a cooling relationship only after work has moved.
approach: The CRM turns contact frequency, meeting density and news into health scores and alerts the owner when a relationship cools.
Howes Percival says DealCloud dashboards and alerts help it keep in touch at the right frequency; no figure (vendor-published).
The relationship owner decides whether and how to act on each alert; leadership decides what a cooling key relationship needs.

title: Account plans and cross-sell lists built from relationship, matter and client data
problem: Key-account plans need data from many practices, and partners say knowing where to focus and spotting cross-sell are among their biggest business development frictions.
approach: AI combines email, CRM records, matter history and client news into account summaries and an opportunity matrix (vendor-described, announced).
No named firm reports AI-built account plans in use; 54% of partners in a survey rank cross-sell the top benefit (vendor-published).
The account team decides plan content; risk or ethics staff check independence and conflicts before a new service is proposed.

title: Scheduled AI scans of courts, news and filings to find new work
problem: Finding new mandates and cross-sell openings means manual searching of court records, news and filings that busy lawyers cannot do consistently.
approach: Tools combine internal relationship and matter data with external sources and return scored opportunities. Akin Gump built 'Moneyball' in-house.
Quinn Emanuel showed daily deep-research prompts scanning appellate decisions and verdicts, scoring matters for 'who pays' and intervention windows.
Lawyers and business development staff evaluate and decide which opportunities to pursue.

title: AI-prepared pre-meeting client briefs for partners and new teams
problem: Preparing for a client meeting means searching the CRM, inboxes, news and filings by hand, and partners with little non-billable time arrive underprepared.
approach: A brief is generated from relationship history, account activity, news and sometimes matter history. Named: Grassi, LBMC, Thomson Snell & Passmore, Practus.
Intapp says briefs that would take hours of research 'can be surfaced in seconds'; no measurement (vendor-published).
The partner reads, interprets and personalises the brief before use; account partners review priorities extracted from matters.
who: Grassi, LBMC, Thomson Snell & Passmore, Practus

title: Business development assistants grounded in firm relationship data, not generic chatbots
problem: Partners take on business development with little time and do not log into the CRM; 68% of those using AI rely only on general-purpose tools.
approach: Vendors connect assistants to governed relationship data: Introhive announced an MCP connector, and Intapp's Celeste answers plain-language questions over relationship history.
Practus, Wotton Kearney and Ropes & Gray announced selecting DealCloud with Celeste. Intapp says 'minutes rather than hours' (vendor claim).
The partner reviews every outbound message; staff review answers before acting.

title: Nudges when a client goes quiet, with draft notes for the partner
problem: Partners know they should contact clients regularly but lack time or a reason, and senior lawyers often skip client notes because writing them takes billable time.
approach: The system prompts the partner when a relationship goes quiet and supplies a draft. Intapp sells DealCloud Activator, with leaderboards for leaders.
AI pulls news and regulatory developments and drafts client alerts (Harvey). An Intapp study links Activator behaviours to up to 32% (vendor-published).
The partner chooses whether to send and edits the draft; a lawyer reviews each client alert.

title: AI call summaries and call coaching filed in the account record
problem: Notes from client calls and meetings are lost or never reach the account record.
approach: A call summary agent turns calls into meeting summaries, and a call coach agent analyses recordings to improve communication.
Both feed the account record in a professional services automation system; Certinia lists them (vendor-published, announced). No figure published.
The account lead reviews the summary before it is filed, and the notetaker is disclosed at the meeting start.

title: Agentic origination and business development playbooks over relationship and intake data
problem: Intapp argues most legal AI speeds up the practice of law for individuals but not the business behind it, and large-firm business workflows are often inefficient.
approach: Intapp's Celeste runs multi-step playbooks for origination, business development, intake, conflicts, pricing and lateral hiring, with a no-code builder.
Intapp says it can surface matters and pitch material in 'minutes rather than hours'. Practus and Wotton Kearney announced selecting it.
Review points in the playbooks are not described in the sources.

title: Idea: agent-run outbound outreach that picks contacts and drafts messages within limits
problem: Idea, not a deployment: partners do not follow up consistently, and business development teams are asked to do more outreach with the same people.
approach: Idea discussed by practitioners: an agent chooses contacts, drafts messages and schedules or sends them within limits, escalating replies to a person.
No firm was found running autonomous outbound outreach; no outcome figure is published.
The partner approves the target list and message templates; a person reviews replies and messages containing client advice.

title: AI capability claims in marketing and thought leadership under editorial control
problem: Clients expect AI-savvy firms and vague messaging is a missed opportunity, but AI claims are regulated as marketing statements and AI-generated content has transparency rules.
approach: Firms describe their AI tools in marketing, grounded in facts. Examples: Akin Gump's 'Moneyball', Debevoise's STAAR platform, Parker Poe's client AI lab.
Drafting that content with AI under editorial control is the proposed method; no firm was found describing it.
A named editor or partner holds editorial responsibility, and marketing or ethics review checks any AI claim.

title: Website chatbot that answers prospective clients, gathers facts and routes leads
problem: Prospects contact firms outside office hours and intake is slow, but a conversational tool can create a client relationship by accident or mislead.
approach: A chatbot answers visitors' questions, gathers facts and routes leads to a lawyer. California names autonomously facilitating client intake as agentic AI.
Bar opinions describe intake chatbots as in use; no named firm or measured result was found.
A responsible lawyer reviews each interaction; lawyer approval is needed before any autonomous communication goes out.

title: Partner-led AI value conversations with key clients, prepared with evidence
problem: Clients want AI-enabled quality and savings but hear little, partners rarely raise it, and firms get contradictory instructions from clients about AI use.
approach: Firms prepare partners with talking points, client insight, approved language and billing guidance, then sequence the conversation from what changed to pricing.
Greenberg Traurig's chief pricing and innovation officer said once-silent clients now ask how AI is used on their matters.
The partner leads and owns what is claimed; pricing proposals go through the firm's pricing function.

title: Matter-level evidence of AI use and its effect, shown to clients
problem: Clients ask what AI did on their matters and what it saved, but firms mostly cannot answer from their records.
approach: Capture AI-assisted work against client and matter so account teams can show where AI was used and what was reviewed.
Legora and Laurel announced on 2026-10-13 that Laurel will turn each Legora task into a draft time entry.
Lawyers review draft time entries; the billing partner approves any AI-related line item or credit.

title: AI disclosure and consent terms in engagement letters and client guideline responses
problem: Clients ask how AI is used on their work and set terms about it, while professional-body guidance says boilerplate consent is not enough.
approach: Firms standardise AI terms (permitted uses, human review, no confidential data in public AI without written consent) in engagement letters.
Babst Calland's published terms say it may use AI with attorney oversight and the client consents by using its services.
A partner or risk lead approves the AI terms for each client; terms are reviewed annually.

title: In-house teams add AI addenda to outside counsel guidelines and panel reviews
problem: Existing outside counsel guidelines predate AI and give clients no control over which AI tools firms use or how output is reviewed; two-thirds of general counsel do not know.
approach: In-house teams add an AI addendum covering permitted tools, no training on client data, written consent for pass-through charges and audit rights.
They also add AI questions to panel reviews; firms must act on these as account requirements. No figure published.
Legal operations and the responsible lawyer decide which tools and uses are permitted, with periodic spot-checks.

title: AI analysis of client feedback, win-loss and matter-close debriefs
problem: Client feedback programmes are periodic, siloed and reach few clients, and informal feedback in meetings and emails goes unrecorded.
approach: AI groups free-text feedback from interviews, surveys and debriefs into one view. Shoosmiths announced in May 2023 it would use MyCustomerLens.
Koji offers AI-moderated client interviews; Shoosmiths' efficiencies are described only qualitatively (self-reported). Current use is not confirmed.
Account leads and senior decision makers review the analysis and decide follow-up.

title: Linking business development activity to revenue
problem: Most firms cannot connect business development activity to revenue, so they cannot show whether relationship tools or AI pay back.
approach: Relationship, pipeline and billing data are joined so introductions and cross-sell can be attributed to revenue. Intapp lists 'outcome attribution' in DealCloud.
A vendor survey says 63% have no revenue-linked way to measure return and 15% track revenue with strong attribution (vendor-published).
Business development and finance leaders agree attribution rules before results are used, especially in partner pay.

title: Co-creating AI with key clients through client AI labs and joint measures
problem: Clients want evidence that a firm's AI helps them, but talk rarely turns into shared work, and neither side has a way to measure or split AI savings.
approach: Parker Poe held a 2026-09-10 workshop where general counsel and executives built AI assistants with its lawyers on Lega's builder lab.
About 90% chose the executive briefing track (self-reported). GSK says it looks to partner with outside firms on new AI use cases.
Lawyers and client staff jointly judge which outputs are useful; both sides sign off use case and measure first.

title: Firm-built AI tools and client portals offered to clients
problem: Clients want AI-enabled service but see little of what firms do, and firms want to stay central as clients adopt AI themselves.
approach: Law firms package knowledge into client tools: Debevoise's STAAR on AI risk, Cooley GO Lab for startups and A&O Shearman's Harvey licensing.
Legora's Portal lets firms invite clients into a white-labelled workspace; some details are announced, not in use; no outcome published.
Firm lawyers curate and review the guidance the tools draw on.

title: Client AI enablement roles that scope and advise on clients' own AI
problem: Clients ask what the firm's AI means for them and bring their own AI to their advisers, but partners lack time or knowledge to scope AI engagements.
approach: A dedicated innovation team supports partners and clients. Latham & Watkins' Innovation Attorney scopes client AI engagements and advises on limits.
No outcome figure is published. Other firms' postings were seen in search only; accounting and consulting uses are event ideas.
Client AI work is delivered with human oversight, and partners lead advice on tools, risks and use cases.
